title: Logistic Regression and Classification
description: The logistic model, cross-entropy loss, gradient and Newton methods, decision boundaries, the perceptron and softmax regression.
overview: Classification asks for a category instead of a number. A linear model's output can be any real number, so we pass it through a function that squashes it into a probability. The result, logistic regression, is the workhorse of classification: it is fast, it is interpretable, and it is the building block of neural networks, whose last layer is usually a logistic or softmax unit.

We derive the model from the idea of log-odds, fit it by maximum likelihood, solve it with gradient ascent and Newton's method, examine the decision boundary, and then extend to the perceptron and to more than two classes.
objectives: Write the logistic model and interpret its output as a probability and its weights as log-odds.
Derive the log-likelihood, its gradient and its Hessian.
Carry out gradient and Newton steps by hand on a small data set.
Describe the decision boundary and explain what happens on linearly separable data.
State the perceptron update, and write the softmax model and its loss for K classes.

sections.title: The logistic model
body: Let y ∈ {0, 1}. Fitting a line to 0/1 labels by least squares is a poor idea: predictions fall outside [0, 1], and a few distant points tilt the line and change the classification of unrelated points. We want a model of the probability P(y = 1 | x).

The trouble is that a weighted sum θᵀx can be any real number, while a probability must lie between 0 and 1. We need a bridge between the two. The bridge goes through odds. The **odds** of an event with probability p are p/(1 − p). A probability of 0.8 means odds of 0.8/0.2 = 4, or "4 to 1 for". A probability of 0.5 gives odds of 1, and a probability of 0.2 gives odds of 0.25. Odds take any positive value, and taking the logarithm turns them into any real value, positive or negative. The **log-odds** (**logit**) is ln(p/(1 − p)). Now the weighted sum can safely be set equal to it. Assume the log-odds are linear in the features:

Solving for p gives the **sigmoid** (logistic function) of θᵀx. It works as a squashing function: large positive scores become probabilities near 1, large negative scores become probabilities near 0, and a score of exactly 0 gives 0.5.

body.caption: The sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^{−z}). It equals 0.5 at z = 0 and saturates at 0 and 1.

list: σ is increasing, σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z), and its derivative is σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), at most 1/4 at z = 0.
The weight θ_j is the change in log-odds per unit change of x_j. Increasing x_j by one multiplies the odds by e^{θ_j}.
The two cases combine into one formula: P(y | x; θ) = h^y (1 − h)^{1−y}.

example.title: From weights to probability
example.problem: A model has θ = (−4, 2) with x = (1, x₁). Find P(y = 1) at x₁ = 3 and the value of x₁ at which the probability is 0.5. By what factor do the odds change when x₁ increases by 1?
solution: The probability is 0.5 when the log-odds are 0: −4 + 2x₁ = 0, so x₁ = 2.
Each unit increase of x₁ multiplies the odds by e² = 7.39.

sections.title: Maximum likelihood and cross-entropy
body: How do we choose θ? Ask which θ makes the labels we actually saw most probable. For a single example with label 1, the model assigns probability h to it, so we want h large. For a label 0 the model assigns 1 − h, so we want h small. For example, with labels (1, 0, 1) and predicted probabilities (0.9, 0.2, 0.7), the probability of seeing exactly these labels is 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.504. Another θ giving (0.6, 0.5, 0.5) scores 0.6 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.15, which is worse. Maximum likelihood picks the θ with the highest such product. Products of many small numbers are awkward, so we take logarithms, which turn the product into a sum without changing which θ is best.
Assuming independent examples, the likelihood of the training labels is the product of the individual probabilities, and the log-likelihood is

Minimizing the average negative log-likelihood, J(θ) = −ℓ(θ)/m, is the same as minimizing the **binary cross-entropy** loss. It penalizes a confident wrong prediction heavily: a true label 1 with predicted probability 0.01 costs −ln 0.01 = 4.6.
Differentiate one term with h = σ(z), z = θᵀx, using σ′ = σ(1 − σ):
Summing over examples,

This has exactly the form of the least squares gradient, with h in place of the linear prediction. That similarity is not an accident; it is a property of all generalized linear models (see the next chapter). Gradient descent is θ ← θ − α ∇J(θ).

example.title: A gradient step
example.problem: The data are x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with labels y = 0, 1, 0, 1, and the model has an intercept. At θ = (0, 0), compute the gradient of the average loss and a descent step with α = 1.
solution: With θ = 0 every probability is 0.5, so h − y = (0.5, −0.5, 0.5, −0.5).
The step gives θ = (0, 0.25): the slope increases, since larger x values tend to have label 1.

body.key: The log-likelihood of logistic regression is concave (equivalently, J is convex), so gradient methods reach the global optimum. There is no closed form, unlike least squares.

check.q: The gradient of the logistic log-likelihood is
check.a: Xᵀ(y − h), where h holds the predicted probabilities
wrong: Σ h x, with no dependence on y

sections.title: Newton's method
body: Gradient descent uses the slope only, so it knows which way is downhill but not how far to go. **Newton's method** also uses the curvature (how quickly the slope itself changes). At each step it replaces J near the current point by the parabola (or its higher-dimensional version) that matches the value, slope and curvature there, then jumps straight to the bottom of that parabola. When J really is close to a parabola, one jump lands very near the minimum. Formally, it minimizes the second-order Taylor approximation of J at each step:
For logistic regression the Hessian has a clean form:

eq: H = (1/m) Xᵀ S X,    S = diag( h_i(1 − h_i) )

body: S has positive diagonal entries, so H is positive semidefinite (J is convex), and each Newton step solves a weighted least squares problem, which is why the method is also called iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS). Near the optimum, Newton's method converges quadratically: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. It typically needs 5 to 10 iterations, versus hundreds for gradient descent. The price is forming and solving with an n×n matrix at every step, O(mn² + n³).

example.title: A Newton step
example.problem: Use the same data (x = 1, 2, 3, 4; y = 0, 1, 0, 1) at θ = (0, 0). Take one Newton step.
solution: All probabilities are 0.5, so S = 0.25 I and H = (0.25/4) XᵀX with X = [[1,1],[1,2],[1,3],[1,4]].

With gradient g = (0, −0.25), H⁻¹g = (2, −0.8), so θ ← (0, 0) − (2, −0.8) = (−2, 0.8). The decision boundary −2 + 0.8x = 0 is at x = 2.5, between the labels as expected. The probabilities are σ(−1.2) = 0.23, σ(−0.4) = 0.40, σ(0.4) = 0.60 and σ(1.2) = 0.77 at x = 1, …, 4, close to optimal in a single step.

body: Newton's method is a second-order method and needs a convex or at least well-behaved function. For high-dimensional problems such as deep networks, quasi-Newton methods and first-order methods are used instead (see Gradient Methods in the Mathematics book).

check.q: Newton's method is attractive for logistic regression because
check.a: J is convex and the method converges in few iterations
wrong: It does not need the gradient
Each iteration is cheaper than a gradient step

sections.title: Decision boundaries and separable data
body: To classify, predict y = 1 when P(y = 1 | x) > 0.5, that is when θᵀx > 0. The **decision boundary** {x : θᵀx = 0} is a hyperplane: a point in one dimension, a line in two, a plane in three. Logistic regression is therefore a **linear classifier**. The vector θ is perpendicular to the boundary, and the distance from a point to the boundary is |θᵀx|/‖θ‖. The probability is the sigmoid of that scaled distance, so points far from the boundary get probabilities near 0 or 1.
Nonlinear boundaries come from feature maps, as in regression: adding x₁², x₂² and x₁x₂ lets a linear classifier in feature space draw an ellipse in the original space.

If a hyperplane separates the two classes perfectly (the data are **linearly separable**), the likelihood can always be increased by scaling θ upward: multiplying θ by c > 1 sharpens every probability toward the correct 0 or 1 and raises ℓ. No finite maximizer exists, the weights grow without bound, and the probabilities become extreme. Gradient descent never converges, and Newton's method hits a singular Hessian.

body.warn: On separable or nearly separable data, always add regularization. The penalty λ‖θ‖² stops the weights from diverging and also improves generalization. Most libraries regularize logistic regression by default.

body: The regularized objective is J(θ) + (λ/2m)‖θ‖² (again with the intercept excluded). It is still convex, and the Gaussian-prior (MAP) interpretation of Regularization applies.

check.q: With θ = (−1, 2, 3) and x = (1, 0, 1), which class is predicted?
Why does unregularized logistic regression fail on linearly separable data?
check.a: The likelihood keeps increasing as the weights grow, so no finite maximizer exists

sections.title: The perceptron
body: The **perceptron** replaces the sigmoid with a hard threshold: h(x) = 1 if θᵀx ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise. It outputs a class but no probability. It was proposed by Rosenblatt in 1958 and is the ancestor of the neural network. Its learning rule has the same form as the logistic update:

The correction is zero when the example is classified correctly. On a mistake with y = 1, h = 0, the update adds αx to θ, which raises θᵀx on that example. On a mistake with y = 0, h = 1, it subtracts αx.

body.key: Perceptron convergence theorem (Novikoff). If every ‖x‖ ≤ R and some unit vector θ* separates the data with margin γ (y θ*ᵀx ≥ γ in ±1 labeling), the perceptron makes at most (R/γ)² mistakes, whatever the order or the number of examples.

body: The bound depends on the geometry (the margin), not on the dimension or the number of examples. If the data are not separable, the perceptron never settles. Large-margin classifiers, which come next in the book, choose the separating hyperplane with the biggest γ, and kernels allow the perceptron in very high dimensions.

example.title: A perceptron update
example.problem: Labels are 0/1, α = 1, θ = (0, 0, 0) and the first example is x = (1, 2, −1) with y = 1. Update θ.
example.solution: θᵀx = 0 ≥ 0, so h = 1, which is correct; no update. For a second example x = (1, −1, 3) with y = 0, h = 1 (since θᵀx = 0) is wrong, so θ ← θ + 1(0 − 1)x = (−1, 1, −3).

check.q: The perceptron mistake bound (R/γ)² depends on
check.a: the radius of the data and the margin

sections.title: More than two classes: softmax regression
body: With K classes, give each class its own weight vector θ_k and score s_k = θ_kᵀx, like K separate judges each rating how well x fits their class. The raw scores can be negative and do not add up to 1, so they are not yet probabilities. The **softmax** fixes this in two steps: exponentiate each score so that it becomes positive, then divide by the total so that they sum to 1. A higher score still means a higher probability, and the exponential makes the leader stand out more:

body.eq: P(y = k | x) = exp(s_k) / Σ_{j=1}^{K} exp(s_j)

body: Probabilities are positive and sum to one. For K = 2 the model reduces to logistic regression, with θ = θ₁ − θ₀. The loss is the cross-entropy: with y one-hot encoded (a vector with a 1 in the true class's position),

eq: loss = − Σ_k y_k ln p_k = − ln p_{true class}

body: The gradient again has the 'prediction minus target' form. Softmax with cross-entropy is the output layer of nearly every neural classifier.

example.title: Softmax probabilities and loss
example.problem: Three classes have scores (2, 1, 0). Find the probabilities. If the true class is the second, what is the loss and the gradient with respect to the scores?
solution: The loss is −ln 0.245 = 1.41. The gradient with respect to the scores is p − y = (0.665, 0.245 − 1, 0.090) = (0.665, −0.755, 0.090): it pushes the true class's score up and the others down.

list: **One-vs-rest**: train K binary classifiers, each separating one class from all the others, and predict the class with the highest score. It needs only a binary learner.
**One-vs-one**: train K(K − 1)/2 classifiers on pairs of classes and vote.
**Numerical stability**: compute softmax as exp(s_k − max_j s_j) / Σ exp(s_j − max s). Subtracting the maximum leaves the result unchanged and avoids overflow.

quiz.q: An event has probability 0.9. Its odds are
quiz.why: Odds = p/(1 − p) = 0.9/0.1 = 9, meaning "9 to 1 for". The value 0.11 is the odds of the complement.

quiz.q: A logistic model gives log-odds of ln 3 for an input. The probability P(y = 1) is
quiz.why: Log-odds ln 3 means odds of 3, so p = odds/(1 + odds) = 3/4 = 0.75.

quiz.q: A weight is θ_j = −0.5. If x_j increases by 2 units, the odds of y = 1 are multiplied by about
quiz.why: Log-odds change by −0.5 × 2 = −1, so the odds are multiplied by e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37. The value 0.61 is e^{−0.5}, the effect of a single unit.

quiz.q: A model has θ = (−6, 3) with x = (1, x₁). At x₁ = 1, P(y = 1) is about
quiz.why: The log-odds are −6 + 3 = −3, so P = σ(−3) = 1/(1 + e³) ≈ 0.047. The value 0.95 is σ(3), with the sign flipped.

quiz.q: Why is least squares on 0/1 labels a poor way to classify?
quiz.a: Predictions leave [0, 1], and distant points can tilt the line and change other points' classes
wrong: The squared error is not differentiable for binary labels
It cannot represent a linear relationship between the features and the label
The normal equations have no solution when y ∈ {0, 1}
quiz.why: The line is unbounded and a far-away point drags it, so it is not a probability model. The normal equations are perfectly solvable.

quiz.q: Labels (1, 1, 0) are given probabilities of class 1 equal to (0.5, 0.8, 0.25). The likelihood of exactly these labels is
quiz.why: Use h for a label 1 and 1 − h for a label 0: 0.5 × 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.30. The value 0.10 forgets that a label 0 contributes 1 − h.

quiz.q: The true label is 0 and the model gives P(y = 1) = 0.9. The cross-entropy for this example is
quiz.why: The model gave the true label probability 0.1, so the loss is −ln 0.1 ≈ 2.30. The value 0.105 is −ln 0.9, the loss if the label were 1.

quiz.q: Data are x = 1, 2 with labels y = 1, 0, and the model has an intercept. Starting from θ = (0, 0) with α = 1, one gradient descent step gives θ =
quiz.why: All h = 0.5, so h − y = (−0.5, 0.5). Then ∂J/∂θ₀ = 0 and ∂J/∂θ₁ = (−0.5 + 1.0)/2 = 0.25, and the step subtracts it. Using a sum instead of the mean gives −0.5.

quiz.q: Why is Newton's method for logistic regression also called iteratively reweighted least squares?
quiz.a: Each step solves a weighted least squares problem with weights h(1 − h)
wrong: It refits the labels from the residuals at each iteration
It restarts from the least squares solution every time
It replaces the sigmoid by a straight line near the optimum
quiz.why: The Hessian is XᵀSX/m with S = diag(h_i(1 − h_i)), so the step is a least squares solve in which each example is weighted by S.

quiz.q: In the Hessian of logistic regression, which example receives the largest weight h(1 − h)?
wrong: All examples receive the same weight
quiz.why: h(1 − h) peaks at h = 0.5, where it equals 0.25, and is tiny for confident predictions at either end.

quiz.q: With θ = (3, −1.5) and x = (1, x₁), the model predicts class 1 when
quiz.why: Class 1 is predicted when θᵀx = 3 − 1.5x₁ > 0, which gives x₁ < 2. The negative weight reverses the usual direction.

quiz.q: A linear classifier is to have a circular boundary in the (x₁, x₂) plane. Which added features make this possible?
quiz.why: A boundary a x₁² + a x₂² + b = 0 is a circle, and it is linear in the new features. The other options still give a straight-line boundary.

quiz.q: On linearly separable data, a fitted θ classifies every point correctly. Multiplying θ by 3 will
quiz.a: raise the log-likelihood while leaving the boundary unchanged
wrong: lower the log-likelihood, since the probabilities become overconfident
leave the log-likelihood unchanged, since the boundary is unchanged
raise it only for the examples nearest the boundary
quiz.why: The boundary θᵀx = 0 does not move, but every correct probability is pushed toward 1, so ℓ keeps increasing. This is why the weights diverge without regularization.

quiz.q: A perceptron with α = 1 has θ = (1, 2, −1) and sees x = (1, 1, 3) with y = 0. The new θ is
quiz.why: θᵀx = 1 + 2 − 3 = 0, so h = 1, which is a mistake. The update is θ + (0 − 1)x = (0, 1, −4), and the new score is −11, which is correct.

quiz.q: All inputs satisfy ‖x‖ ≤ 5 and the data have margin γ = 0.5. The perceptron makes at most how many mistakes?
quiz.why: The bound is (R/γ)² = (5/0.5)² = 100. It holds whatever the number of examples or features.

quiz.q: A softmax model with two classes has scores (3, 1). The probability of the first class is about
quiz.why: e³/(e³ + e¹) = 1/(1 + e⁻²) = σ(2) ≈ 0.881, so softmax with two classes is logistic regression on the score difference. The 0.75 comes from the unexponentiated 3/4.

quiz.q: Softmax probabilities are (0.2, 0.7, 0.1) and the true class is the second. The cross-entropy gradient with respect to the scores is
quiz.why: The gradient is p − y with y one-hot: (0.2, 0.7 − 1, 0.1). It raises the true class's score and lowers the others.

quiz.q: A problem has K = 6 classes. How many binary classifiers does the one-vs-one approach train?
quiz.why: One-vs-one trains K(K − 1)/2 = 15 classifiers, one per pair, whereas one-vs-rest trains K = 6.

summary: Logistic regression models P(y = 1 | x) = σ(θᵀx), equivalently linear log-odds. Weights multiply the odds by e^{θ_j} per unit of x_j.
Maximum likelihood gives the cross-entropy loss. Its gradient is Xᵀ(h − y)/m, and J is convex, with no closed form.
Newton's method uses H = XᵀSX/m with S = diag(h(1 − h)) and converges in a few steps.
The decision boundary θᵀx = 0 is a hyperplane. On separable data the unregularized weights diverge, so regularize.
The perceptron is the hard-threshold version with the update θ ← θ + α(y − h)x, and makes at most (R/γ)² mistakes on separable data.
Softmax regression generalizes to K classes with cross-entropy loss and gradient (p − y)xᵀ.
